title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Macrocytic. MCV > 100; > 120 suggests megaloblastic anaemia from B12 or folate deficiency.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Starting point. Confirm anaemia by WHO criteria, then classify by MCV and reticulocyte count.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Microcytic, hypochromic. Low MCV, MCH and MCHC; iron deficiency is by far the most common cause; ferritin distinguishes it.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Normocytic, normochromic. Reticulocytes separate regenerative causes (bleeding, haemolysis) from central ones (marrow failure).
Significant fall in Hb for age and sex; WHO: < 13 g/dL men, < 12 g/dL women.
Fatigue, dyspnoea, dizziness, palpitations, pulsatile tinnitus, headache, chest pain, pallor or jaundice.
CBC with indices, reticulocytes, smear; ferritin/iron, B12, folate, LDH, bilirubin, haptoglobin, Coombs, Hb electrophoresis, TSH, creatinine, marrow.
Microcytic (iron deficiency, chronic disease, thalassaemia, sideroblastic); normocytic (bleeding, haemolysis, marrow failure); macrocytic (B12/folate, hypothyroidism, myelodysplasia, drugs).
Microcytic hypochromic anaemia, normal WBC/platelets, low ferritin; pica; treat the cause.
Adults 100-200 mg/day (or 60-100 mg alternate days); child 3-6 mg/kg; empty stomach with vitamin C; continue 2-3 months after Hb normalises.
Reticulocytosis in 5-10 days; Hb +1-2 g/dL in 2-4 weeks; correction by 6-8 weeks.
B12 deficiency (pernicious anaemia, gastrectomy, ileal disease, vegan diet), folate deficiency (alcohol, pregnancy, malabsorption), drugs, copper deficiency.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Homocysteine. Accumulates when B12 or folate is lacking.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Methionine synthase. Uses vitamin B12 to transfer the methyl group from 5-methyl-THF to homocysteine.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: 5-methyltetrahydrofolate. Inactive transport form of folate in plasma; must be demethylated to join DNA synthesis.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Tetrahydrofolate. Active folate, converted to 5,10-methylene-THF, the one-carbon donor for thymidine.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Thymidylate synthase. Converts dUMP to dTMP for DNA; without it nuclei mature slowly while cytoplasm matures normally (megaloblastosis).

title: Common role of B9 and B12?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: Common role of B9 and B12?
body.back: DNA synthesis; deficiency causes nucleo-cytoplasmic asynchrony and megaloblastic anaemia.
Pteridine + PABA + glutamate; leafy vegetables and liver; destroyed by heat.
330 µg/day (440 in pregnancy); duodenum/jejunum; circulates as 5-methyl-THF; liver stores last months.
Methionine synthase (B12) converts 5-methyl-THF to THF and homocysteine to methionine; THF → 5,10-methylene-THF for thymidylate synthase.
Corrin ring with cobalt; animal foods only.
Binds intrinsic factor (parietal cells), absorbed in terminal ileum, carried by transcobalamin; liver stores last years.
Pernicious anaemia, gastrectomy, ileal resection/disease, vegan diet.

title: Why not give folate alone in B12 deficiency?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: Why not give folate alone in B12 deficiency?
body.back: It corrects the anaemia but not the neurological damage, which can progress.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Primary haemostasis defect. Mucocutaneous bleeding: think thrombocytopenia, platelet function disorder or von Willebrand disease.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Secondary haemostasis defect. Deep bleeding into joints, muscles and body cavities: think coagulation factor deficiency such as haemophilia.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: First-line tests. Screening panel guided by the history; beware pre-analytical errors.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Second-line tests. Specific tests for von Willebrand disease, platelet function and factor levels, plus mixing studies.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Third-line tests. Specialised assays for inhibitors and fibrinolysis.
Subjective histories and symptoms taken as normal; they are the second most common haematology consultation.
Type and site, spontaneous vs traumatic, duration (lifelong vs recent), surgery/extractions, transfusions, drugs (aspirin, NSAIDs), family history, consanguinity.
Primary: petechiae, ecchymoses, epistaxis, gums, haematuria, melaena. Secondary: haematomas, haemarthrosis, muscle, cavity and CNS bleeding.
ISTH Bleeding Assessment Tool (paediatric version too) standardises and objectifies bleeding history.
1st: CBC, PFA-100/bleeding time, PT, aPTT, fibrinogen. 2nd: VWF antigen/activity, aggregometry, FVIII/FIX, mixing. 3rd: inhibitors, α2-antiplasmin, PAI-1.
General (vaccination, avoid NSAIDs, gynaecological evaluation), local pressure, tranexamic acid, hormonal therapy, replacement of the missing factor.
Type 1 reduced VWF (most common), type 2 dysfunctional (4 subtypes), type 3 absent (rare, severe).
History, ISTH-BAT, CBC, coagulation, VWF antigen, VWF activity, FVIII; education, tranexamic acid, desmopressin, VWF/FVIII-VWF concentrates, prophylaxis.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Red cell indices. MCV classifies anaemia (micro, normo, macrocytic); MCH and MCHC assess colour; RDW measures size variation (anisocytosis).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Platelets and rare white cells. Thrombocytopenia < 150, thrombocytosis > 400 G/L; eosinophilia > 0.4 and basophilia > 0.1 G/L.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Red cell values. RBC count, haemoglobin and haematocrit quantify red cells; anaemia is Hb < 13 in men and < 12 in women.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: White cells. Total count and differential, always interpreted in absolute values.

title: What is a CBC and why is it done?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is a CBC and why is it done?
body.back: Quantitative and qualitative count of red cells, white cells and platelets; assesses haematopoiesis; indications: infection, anaemia, bleeding, tumour, thrombosis, pregnancy, surgery.
Venous blood in EDTA (lavender) tube, mixed; reject clotted or > 48 h samples.
Hb men 13-16.5, women 12-16 g/dL; Hct 40-50% / 35-45%; RBC men 5-5.5, women 4-4.5 million/mm³.
MCV 80-98 fL (< 80 micro, > 100 macro); MCH 27-32 pg; MCHC 32-36 g/dL; RDW 11.5-14.5% (> 15 anisocytosis).
Anisocytosis (size), poikilocytosis (shape: spherocytes, target cells, sickle cells, schistocytes), hypochromia.
WBC 4-10; neutrophils 1.8-7; lymphocytes 1.5-4; monocytes 0.2-0.8; eosinophils < 0.4; basophils < 0.1 G/L.
< 1.5 G/L neutropenia; < 0.5 G/L agranulocytosis.
150-400 G/L; pregnancy lowers Hb (≥ 11 accepted) and raises neutrophils; newborns have high Hb and MCV; smoking raises neutrophils.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Common pathway. Factor Xa with cofactor Va, calcium and phospholipids (prothrombinase) converts prothrombin to thrombin.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Extrinsic pathway. Tissue factor exposed by injury binds factor VIIa; the main initiator in vivo; explored by the prothrombin time (factors VII, X, V, II, I).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Fibrin. Thrombin cleaves fibrinogen to fibrin and activates factor XIII, which cross-links it into a stable clot.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Natural anticoagulants. Antithrombin inactivates thrombin, IXa, Xa, XIa, XIIa (boosted by heparin); activated protein C with protein S inactivates Va and VIIIa; TFPI blocks TF-VIIa.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Intrinsic pathway. Contact activation of XII, then XI, IX with cofactor VIII (tenase); explored by the aPTT.
Cascade of enzyme activations where plasma proteins, tissue factor and calcium interact on platelets to form fibrin.
Zymogens (serine proteases), 'a' = active; mostly liver-made; V and VIII labile cofactors; TF main in vivo initiator.
II, VII, IX, X, proteins C and S; warfarin or deficiency → inactive PIVKA.
Extrinsic: TF + VIIa. Intrinsic: XII, XI, IX + VIII (tenase). Common: Xa + Va (prothrombinase) → thrombin → fibrin; XIII cross-links.
XII/PK/HMWK deficiency → no bleeding; XI deficiency mild; haemophilia A/B cannot bypass via the other pathway.
Initiation (TF-VIIa → IX, X, little thrombin), amplification (V, VIII, XI, platelets), propagation (thrombin burst), stabilisation (XIIIa).
Antithrombin (+ heparin): thrombin, IXa, Xa, XIa, XIIa. Protein C + S: Va, VIIIa. TFPI: TF-VIIa.
Citrate 3.2%, 9:1, no clot or heparin; PT (extrinsic + common), aPTT (intrinsic + common), TT, fibrinogen; then factor assays, mixing studies.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Haematopoietic growth factors. Act through surface receptors: multilineage early factors and lineage-specific ones.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Haematopoietic stem cell. Multipotent, self-renewing, low mitotic activity; looks like a large lymphocyte; identified only by surface markers (CD).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Mature cells. Red cells (120 days), platelets (7-10 days), white cells (days in blood).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Precursors (blasts). Proerythroblasts, myeloblasts, megakaryoblasts, lymphoblasts, monoblasts: recognisable on smears, one lineage each.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Progenitors. Common myeloid (CMP) and common lymphoid (CLP) progenitors, then MEP, GMP and CFUs; committed, highly mitotic, less self-renewal.

title: Define haematopoiesis and why it is vital.
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: Define haematopoiesis and why it is vital.
body.back: Production of all blood cells from HSCs; mature cells live briefly and cannot divide, while numbers must stay constant.
10¹¹-10¹² cells/day; RBC 120 d, platelets 7-10 d, WBC days.
Embryo: yolk sac, AGM. Fetus: liver, placenta, then spleen and marrow. After birth: bone marrow (axial skeleton).
Return to liver and spleen in marrow failure (thalassaemia, myelofibrosis) → hepatosplenomegaly.
Multipotency, self-renewal, low mitotic activity, not morphologically identifiable (CD markers).
Progenitors: committed (CMP, CLP), mitotic, not identifiable. Precursors: blasts, unilineage, identifiable, no self-renewal.
Early: SCF, IL-3, GM-CSF, IL-7. Lineage-specific: EPO, TPO, G-CSF, M-CSF.
Complete blood count, blood film, bone marrow smear, bone marrow biopsy, flow cytometry.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Secondary haemostasis. A cascade of clotting factors converts fibrinogen to fibrin, stabilising the plug into a clot.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Fibrinolysis. Plasmin dissolves the clot as the vessel heals.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Hypercoagulability. Inherited or acquired thrombophilia raises the risk of stroke, DVT, pulmonary embolism, MI.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Hypocoagulability. Deficient platelets or factors lead to bleeding.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Primary haemostasis. Platelets adhere to exposed subendothelium via von Willebrand factor, activate and aggregate into a plug.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Vasoconstriction. The injured vessel narrows immediately, reducing blood flow.
Normal response to vessel injury: vasoconstriction, platelet plug (primary), fibrin clot (secondary), fibrinolysis; keeps blood fluid elsewhere.
Bleeding (haemophilia, von Willebrand disease, thrombocytopenia) or thrombosis (factor V Leiden, protein C deficiency, cancer, sepsis).
Anucleate megakaryocyte fragments; 150-400 G/L; 8-10 days; 2/3 circulating, 1/3 splenic; destroyed in spleen.
Proliferation, endomitosis, cytoplasmic maturation; ~2,000 platelets per megakaryocyte; TPO from the liver.
Membrane with GPIb, GPIIb-IIIa, GPVI and antigens; canalicular system; cytoskeleton; α-granules (VWF, fibrinogen, PF4); dense granules (ADP, ATP, Ca²⁺, serotonin).
Endothelium thromboresistant (heparan sulfate, inhibitors); injured endothelium and subendothelium prothrombotic (VWF, collagen, tissue factor).
Large multimer from endothelium and megakaryocytes; carries factor VIII; bridges platelet GPIb to collagen.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Buffy coat. Thin layer of leukocytes and platelets between plasma and red cells.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Plasma. Liquid part: water with proteins, electrolytes, nutrients, hormones and waste; serum is plasma without clotting factors.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Red cells. The heaviest cells sink to the bottom; their share of blood volume is the haematocrit.
Branch of medicine studying blood cells, coagulation, blood-forming organs and blood diseases.
Cellular haematology, haemostasis, immuno-haematology, haematological semiology.
Humours and bloodletting; microscope (van Leeuwenhoek); 19th-century descriptions of pernicious anaemia and Hodgkin disease; liver treatment; automation and molecular biology.
~8% body weight, viscosity ~5× water, pH 7.35-7.45, specific gravity 1.055, osmolarity ~300 mOsm, salinity 0.9%.
Plasma ~55%; formed elements ~45%: red cells, white cells, platelets.
Transport (gases, nutrients, hormones, waste), regulation (pH, temperature, fluid), protection (immunity, clotting).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Erythroid use. Transferrin receptor 1 on erythroid precursors takes up iron for haemoglobin.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Dietary iron. Haem iron (meat, Fe²⁺, ~20% absorbed) and non-haem iron (vegetables, Fe³⁺, 1-4% absorbed).

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Absorption. In the duodenum and proximal jejunum: Fe³⁺ reduced by DcytB, taken up by DMT1; exported by ferroportin and oxidised by hephaestin.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Hepcidin. Liver hormone that degrades ferroportin, reducing absorption and release; rises with iron excess and inflammation.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Recycling. Macrophages degrade old red cells and return iron to transferrin: the main daily source of plasma iron.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Storage. Ferritin (soluble, mobilisable) and haemosiderin (insoluble), mainly in liver, spleen and marrow.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Transferrin. Liver-made plasma carrier; each molecule binds two Fe³⁺.

title: Why iron balance is regulated at absorption?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: Why iron balance is regulated at absorption?
body.back: The body cannot produce or actively excrete iron: 4-5 g total in a nearly closed system.
Functional: Hb 60-75%, myoglobin, enzymes. Storage: ferritin, haemosiderin. Transport: transferrin 0.1%.
Diet 15-20 mg; ~10% (1-2 mg) absorbed; 1-2 mg lost.
Haem: Fe²⁺, meat, ~20% absorbed. Non-haem: Fe³⁺, plants, 1-4%; ↑ vitamin C, ↓ tannins.
Duodenum: DcytB reduces Fe³⁺, DMT1 imports; ferroportin exports; hephaestin oxidises; transferrin binds.
Transferrin (liver) carries 2 Fe³⁺; TfR1 on cells (especially erythroid) takes it up; both recycled.
Liver hormone degrading ferroportin; ↑ in overload/inflammation, ↓ in deficiency and active erythropoiesis.
Serum iron, transferrin/TIBC, transferrin saturation, ferritin (stores), Perls stain.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Lymphadenopathy. Enlargement of a lymph node whatever the cause, usually above 1 cm; soft flat submandibular nodes < 1 cm and inguinal nodes up to 2 cm can be normal.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Biopsy triggers. Hard, irregular or fixed node, size above 3 cm, persistence beyond 4-6 weeks, or no diagnosis after 4 weeks of work-up.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Generalized lymphadenopathy. Two or more non-contiguous areas (about a quarter of cases); suggests a systemic disease and usually needs CBC, ESR, CRP and imaging.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Inflammatory node. Tender, warm, soft node with an infection in the drained area (tonsillitis, abscess, genital infection); always think of tuberculosis.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Localized lymphadenopathy. One node area or two adjacent areas (about three quarters of cases in primary care); look at the organs the area drains.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Systemic causes. With an infectious or inflammatory context: mononucleosis, toxoplasmosis, HIV, drugs, autoimmune disease; without one: lymphomas and leukaemias.

title: Define lymphadenopathy and its two forms.
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: Define lymphadenopathy and its two forms.
body.back: Node enlargement (> 1 cm) of any cause; localized = 1 area or 2 adjacent; generalized = ≥ 2 non-contiguous areas.
Soft flat submandibular nodes < 1 cm and inguinal nodes up to 2 cm; normal nodes elsewhere are not palpable.
Cervical: head, neck, thyroid, scalp. Axillary: arm, breast. Inguinal: leg, genitals, anus, lower abdomen. Supraclavicular: thorax, abdomen.
Reactive lymphocyte proliferation, macrophage accumulation, lymphoma, metastasis of a non-lymphoid cancer.
Age, size, quality (tender, hard, fixed, fistulising), time course, localized vs generalized.
Hard, irregular or fixed node; > 3 cm; persisting > 4-6 weeks; or no diagnosis after 4 weeks of work-up.
Right: lung and mediastinum. Left: abdominal cancers (stomach, pancreas, testis, ovary, kidney).
Mononucleosis, toxoplasmosis, HIV, phenytoin or carbamazepine, autoimmune disease; lymphomas and leukaemias.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Above 50,000/µL. Minor surgery generally safe.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: 20,000-50,000/µL. Risk with trauma or invasive procedures.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Below 20,000/µL. Epistaxis, gum bleeding, menorrhagia.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Below 10,000/µL. Risk of gastrointestinal and intracranial haemorrhage; prophylactic transfusion in stable patients.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Three mechanisms. Often combined; the rest of the blood count and the smear point to the cause.
< 150,000/µL; > 50,000 usually safe; 20-50k bleeding with trauma; < 20k spontaneous mucosal; < 10k life-threatening.
Petechiae, ecchymoses, epistaxis, gum bleeding, menorrhagia, GI bleeding, haematuria, intracranial haemorrhage; mucocutaneous pattern.
↓ production (aplasia, MDS, drugs, HIV, EBV, B12/folate), ↑ destruction (ITP, quinine, heparin, sepsis, DIC), sequestration (hypersplenism).
EDTA-induced clumping; smear shows clumps; citrate-tube recount normal; rule out first.
Isolated → ITP; pancytopenia → marrow failure/leukaemia; schistocytes → DIC; giant platelets → Bernard-Soulier; blasts → leukaemia.
Treat the cause; prednisone for ITP; transfusion thresholds < 10k, < 20k, < 50k, < 75k, < 100k.
Reactive (> 80%): infection, inflammation, iron deficiency, splenectomy, surgery. Clonal (< 20%): persistent, thrombosis, splenomegaly, raised Hct/WBC.
CBC + smear, ferritin + CRP, refer if persistent; reactive → treat cause, no aspirin; clonal → low-dose aspirin ± cytoreduction.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Activation. Dense granules release ADP, calcium and serotonin; α-granules release VWF, fibrinogen, PF4; thromboxane A2 is made; phosphatidylserine flips outward for coagulation factors.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Adhesion. After injury, von Willebrand factor bridges exposed collagen to the platelet receptor GPIb; platelets turn from discs into spiky spheres.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Aggregation. Activated GPIIb/IIIa receptors bind fibrinogen, which links neighbouring platelets into the primary plug.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Aspirin. Acetylates COX-1 permanently; anucleate platelets cannot replace it, so the effect lasts their lifespan.

title: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Inherited defects. Bernard-Soulier syndrome lacks GPIb (adhesion); Glanzmann thrombasthenia lacks GPIIb/IIIa (aggregation); von Willebrand disease lacks functional VWF.
Rapid localised plug at injury; maintain fluid, clot-free blood elsewhere and after healing.
Formation of a temporary platelet plug (bricks) later reinforced by fibrin (mortar).
Membrane (TXA2, PAF, PF3), GPIb (VWF), GPIIb/IIIa (fibrinogen), canalicular system, cytoskeleton, α-granules, dense granules.
VWF: carries factor VIII, bridges collagen to GPIb. Fibrinogen: bridges GPIIb/IIIa in aggregation; becomes fibrin in coagulation.

title: Three steps of the platelet plug?
subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: Three steps of the platelet plug?
body.back: Adhesion (GPIb-VWF-collagen), activation (shape change, granule release, TXA2, PS flip, recruitment), aggregation (GPIIb/IIIa-fibrinogen).
Phospholipase A2 → arachidonic acid → COX-1 → PGH2 → TXA2; aspirin irreversibly blocks COX-1 for the platelet lifespan (~10 days).
Thrombocytopenia < 150,000 (marrow failure, peripheral destruction); thrombocytosis > 400,000 (inflammation, splenectomy, essential thrombocythaemia).
Glanzmann thrombasthenia (GPIIb/IIIa), Bernard-Soulier syndrome (GPIb), von Willebrand disease (VWF).

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Hypersplenism. Consequence of any big spleen: pooling and destruction give mild cytopenias with a hypercellular marrow, reversed by splenectomy.

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Hyperplasia or hypertrophy. Reticulo-endothelial work (haemolytic anaemias), immune stimulation (infections, autoimmune disease) or extramedullary haematopoiesis.

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Infiltration. Malignant cells (leukaemias, lymphomas, myeloproliferative neoplasms) or non-malignant material (Gaucher, Niemann-Pick, amyloidosis).

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Splenomegaly. Enlargement beyond normal size (about 12 × 7 cm, < 250 g); a normal spleen is not palpable, so a palpable spleen always needs a cause.
Normal spleen not palpable; splenomegaly is palpable; a palpable spleen is always pathological and needs a cause.
About 12 × 7 cm, under 250 g, along the 9th-11th left ribs, notched anterior edge, moves with inspiration.

body.back: Platelet concentrate. About 40 mL and 5.5 × 10^10 platelets, stored 5 days at 22 °C with gentle agitation; an adult needs 6-8 pooled units.

body.back: Platelet-rich plasma. The supernatant after a soft spin; a hard spin then separates platelets from plasma.

subject: subj:hemato1

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Red cell concentrate. 150-200 mL, about 55 g of haemoglobin, haematocrit 65-80%, stored 42 days at +4 °C; used for anaemia.

body.front: What is at the arrow, and why does it matter?
body.back: Whole blood donation. 400-500 mL collected from a healthy, unpaid, anonymous volunteer after the medical pre-donation interview.
Inherited presence or absence of antigens (glycoproteins or glycolipids) on the red cell surface, recognised by antibodies.
Natural: without exposure (IgM). Regular: always present when the antigen is absent (ABO). Immune: after transfusion or pregnancy (IgG, e.g. anti-D).
A: anti-B. B: anti-A. AB: none. O: anti-A + anti-B. Frequencies A 45%, O 43%, B 9%, AB 3%.

body.front: Why does anti-D matter in pregnancy?
body.back: IgG anti-D in a D-negative mother crosses the placenta and destroys D-positive fetal red cells: haemolytic disease of the newborn.
Strict identification; two typings on two samples; Beth-Vincent (antigens) and Simonin (antibodies) must agree.
